title: Indian Migrant First Person Charged Under UK's New Online Immigration Crime Law
excerpt: Hem Raj, 24, was arrested in Smethwick over social media posts allegedly coaching migrants on fraudulent visa and asylum applications.
body:
• Hem Raj, 24, an Indian national living in Smethwick, is the first person charged under Section 17 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 for advertising illegal immigration services online.
  • He was arrested on September 15 after investigators found social media posts allegedly advising migrants on fraudulent visa applications and asylum claims.
  • Raj was also charged with illegally providing immigration advice under the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, and received conditional bail ahead of a crown court appearance next month.
  • The NCA says it removed nearly 10,700 criminal immigration posts, pages and accounts from social media in the year to December 2025.

The UK's newest immigration offence has its first defendant. Hem Raj, a 24-year-old Indian national living in Smethwick in the West Midlands, has been charged with advertising illegal immigration services online — the first use of Section 17 of the Border Security, Asylum and Immigration Act 2025 in a National Crime Agency case.

Raj was arrested at an address in Smethwick on Tuesday, September 15, in a joint operation by the NCA and West Midlands Police. Investigators found social media posts allegedly offering advice on entering Britain illegally, including guidance on making fraudulent visa applications and claiming asylum after arrival. Mobile phones were seized in the raid.

A new law, tested for the first time

Section 17 criminalises creating or publishing material — online — that promotes unlawful immigration services, carrying fines and prison sentences of up to five years. The offence was designed for exactly this kind of case: posts that coach migrants on breaching immigration law, which the Home Office says reached around 80% of small-boat arrivals through social media channels.

Raj faces a second charge as well: illegally providing immigration advice in contravention of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999, which restricts who may advise on immigration matters in the UK.

"Tackling organised immigration crime remains a top priority for the National Crime Agency, and we are doing all we can to disrupt and dismantle those involved. This includes targeting those who facilitate offending using online platforms."

— Kevin Broadhead, NCA branch commander

A wider sweep of online smugglers

The charge is the sharp end of a much larger enforcement push. The NCA scans social media for potentially criminal material and, working with platforms, removed nearly 10,700 accounts, pages and posts in the twelve months to December 2025 — up from about 8,000 the year before, and more than 27,000 since cooperation with tech firms began.

The Labour government has faced sustained pressure over irregular migration, with small-boat arrivals a defining political issue. Ministers have also rolled out a separate sanctions regime allowing asset freezes, travel bans and financial-system blocks on people enabling irregular migration.

What it means for the community

For Britain's Indian community, the case is a cautionary headline. Immigration solicitors note that social media is full of unregulated advisers offering visa help — and that advice built on false documents puts the migrant's own status at severe risk. Raj received conditional bail and is due to appear at crown court next month, where the new offence will face its first real judicial test.

nri_angle: The case is a warning to diaspora communities where unregulated 'agents' operate on social media — fraudulent advice can now mean a criminal record under Britain's new online-advertising offence.
